frameworks.name: Three Lead Magnet Types
frameworks.definition: A taxonomy of lead magnets: (1) Reveal a problem — surface a problem the prospect didn't know was bad; (2) Free trial — give the solution then remove it to create deprivation; (3) One step of many — solve the first step of a multi-step process that your core offer completes.

frameworks.name: Four Lead Magnet Delivery Formats
frameworks.definition: Four delivery vehicles for lead magnets: software/tools, information (guides, courses, templates), services (done-for-you work for qualified prospects), and physical products; combinations are permitted and often more compelling.

frameworks.name: Lead Magnet Naming Conventions
frameworks.definition: Four headline formulas that increase lead magnet opt-in rates: (1) Number + outcome + timeframe; (2) How to X without Y even if Z; (3) Adjective + type + outcome; (4) X mistakes that prevent good thing.

frameworks.name: CTA Formula (Clear-Action-Reason)
frameworks.definition: A three-part call-to-action structure: (1) clear directive (not clever), (2) exact next action, (3) a reason to act now — any reason outperforms no reason, with genuine scarcity or urgency being strongest.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most website visitors who see only a book-a-call or submit-for-quote CTA are not ready to buy and therefore leave without converting, because those CTAs only work for audiences that are already informed and warm — cold or low-awareness traffic requires a lower-barrier reason to exchange contact information.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Cold or low-awareness inbound traffic
Audience has not previously received value from the sender
claims.mechanism: A cold visitor has no prior relationship with the brand; asking for purchase commitment before establishing value fails to match the visitor's readiness stage, causing them to leave without converting.
bounded_by: Does not apply to warm audiences who already know the brand and have consumed prior content

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that inserting a free mini-offer (lead magnet) between cold traffic and the core offer produces 3-5x more leads than asking directly for a purchase, without increasing advertising spend, because a zero-cost exchange lowers the commitment barrier enough for a much larger fraction of visitors to raise their hand.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Cold or semi-warm traffic
Lead magnet solves a problem related to but distinct from the core offer
claims.mechanism: A zero-cost exchange lowers commitment barrier, allowing more visitors to opt in; subsequent delivery of value creates goodwill and deprivation that converts them to paid buyers.

numbers.axis: Lead volume multiplier from inserting a lead magnet before the core offer CTA

anchors.region: Free lead magnet CTA inserted first

bounded_by: Applies only when the lead magnet is congruent with the core offer; unrelated lead magnets attract wrong audience
Does not increase traffic — only conversion rate of existing traffic

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that improving lead magnet conversion through a better headline — not better content — can increase opt-in rates by 2x, 3x, or 10x, because the packaging determines whether someone wants the magnet before they ever consume it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: wrapping or the packaging of a lead magnet
conditions: Contents already solve a genuine problem for the target audience
Headline is compared against alternative headlines via split testing or polling
claims.mechanism: Prospects judge lead magnets entirely on the headline before opting in; superior packaging raises desire without any change to the underlying content.

numbers.axis: Opt-in rate multiplier from changing the lead magnet headline only

bounded_by: Headline superiority only holds if contents actually solve the stated problem; misleading headlines damage trust and conversion downstream

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the Reveal-a-Problem lead magnet type is the most effective when the underlying problem gets worse with time (e.g., posture, termites, financial delinquency), because discovering the problem creates deprivation that intensifies every second the prospect delays action.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: The problem visibly worsens over time without intervention
The core offer solves the revealed problem
claims.mechanism: Awareness of a worsening problem triggers increasing deprivation; the growing gap between current state and desired state creates urgency that collapses the time-to-purchase.
bounded_by: Less effective for static problems with no deterioration dynamic

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a free trial lead magnet works by giving the solution temporarily and then removing it to create deprivation, and that the key design constraint is limiting some dimension of the offer — number of uses, quantity, or time — to manufacture the moment of deprivation that triggers purchase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product or service is experiential — i.e., the prospect must use it to desire continued access
Removal of access is technically and operationally enforceable
claims.mechanism: Exposure creates desire; removal creates deprivation; deprivation triggers willingness to pay that did not exist before the free trial.
bounded_by: Does not apply to one-time consumable products where the act of consumption eliminates ongoing desire

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that offering free services as a lead magnet is financially justified when the hard cost of delivering that service is low relative to the customer acquisition value — specifically, when giving away a $250-value service at $25 hard cost and converting 1 in 4 recipients, the effective customer acquisition cost is $100, which is acceptable if customer LTV substantially exceeds $100.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Free services given only to qualified prospects (budget, authority, need, timing)
Hard cost of service delivery is substantially below market price
Customer LTV materially exceeds the implied CAC
claims.mechanism: Service delivery builds goodwill and demonstrates competence; qualified prospects who receive real value are substantially more likely to purchase than cold outreach targets.

numbers.axis: Cost-per-acquisition math for free-service lead magnet

bounded_by: Economics collapse if free services are given to unqualified leads (wrong avatar, no budget, no authority)
Does not apply when hard cost of service delivery approaches or exceeds implied customer value

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that lead magnets must not solve the same problem the core offer solves, because doing so satisfies the prospect's need before the pitch, eliminating purchase motivation — analogous to eating an entree and then being offered a second entree.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: deprivation is triggered by solving the first issue
conditions: Lead magnet and core offer exist in the same problem space
claims.mechanism: Satisfying a need removes the deprivation state that motivates purchase; the lead magnet must solve a related but distinct sub-problem that reveals or amplifies the need the core offer addresses.
bounded_by: Does not apply when core offer is a continuation/upgrade of the same product (e.g., free trial → paid subscription)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a prospect pays with time (consuming a lead magnet), they are more likely to subsequently pay with money, because time investment signals intent and creates psychological commitment that lowers resistance to a related purchase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Lead magnet is consumed, not merely downloaded
Core offer is logically adjacent to the lead magnet topic
claims.mechanism: Time investment is a form of psychological commitment; having already invested, the prospect's cognitive consistency bias raises willingness to make the follow-on monetary investment.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that poor lead magnet results indicate that specific lead magnet is flawed — not that the lead magnet strategy is flawed — because lead magnets as a category produce reliable results when the specific packaging, targeting, and problem-solution fit are correct.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that using any reason — even an arbitrary one — in a call-to-action produces higher compliance than no reason, and that genuine scarcity or urgency produces higher compliance still, because the human cognitive system treats the presence of a causal justification as a sufficient reason to comply regardless of the reason's logical merit.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: CTA is already clear and includes exact next action
Reason is stated explicitly, not implied
claims.mechanism: Research on compliance (referenced in transcript: university line-cutting study) shows that the word because triggers automatic compliance even when the stated reason is logically irrelevant; genuine scarcity/urgency amplifies the effect.
bounded_by: Arbitrary reasons erode trust over long-term relationships; genuine scarcity/urgency is preferred for repeat audiences

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that salespeople who ask for the sale most times get the most deals, and that in content marketing, repeated CTAs interspersed with value delivery maximize the cumulative ask rate without fatiguing the audience, because the audience tolerates repeated asks proportional to the value received between asks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: ask as many times as you can
conditions: Value is delivered between each ask
CTAs are clear and direct, not manipulative
claims.mechanism: Ask frequency is bounded by value-per-second delivered to the audience; continuous value delivery increases the audience's tolerance for repeated purchase invitations.
bounded_by: Asking without interspersed value causes audience to disengage and removes the opportunity to ask at all

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for service businesses — which represent approximately 78% of all businesses — genuine capacity scarcity almost always exists and should be stated explicitly in CTAs, because even small operators have a real maximum number of customers they can serve, which creates legitimate urgency.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business is a service business (not self-serve software or physical products)
Scarcity stated is real, not manufactured
claims.mechanism: Service businesses have fixed labor capacity; stating that limit creates honest urgency that prospects accept because they understand service constraints intuitively.

numbers.axis: Prevalence of service businesses among all businesses

bounded_by: Large businesses with genuine excess capacity cannot honestly claim slot scarcity; they can instead use cohort-rollover framing (e.g., limited spots per weekly cohort)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for long-form content like books, the headline and cover design dominate short-term sales volume, but the content between front and back cover determines long-term sales through word-of-mouth — and that anyone can launch a book, while very few can launch a book that continues to sell.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Book or long-form content product
bounded_by: Short-term and long-term drivers are distinct; optimizing only for launch (headline) without substance fails the long-term compounding effect

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that qualifying prospects before delivering a free lead magnet — via a simple conditional redirect based on a qualification dropdown — eliminates freebie-seekers without sacrificing the lead volume benefit of the lead magnet strategy, because only qualified prospects reach the high-value free offer while unqualified ones are redirected to a different (lower-value or unrelated) path.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Lead magnet is offered on a website or landing page
Qualification criteria are answerable by a simple form field (budget, role, readiness)
claims.mechanism: Routing logic at the form level filters on qualification before granting access; qualified leads receive the high-value magnet while unqualified leads are not exposed to it.
bounded_by: Requires clear, binary qualification criteria; fuzzy criteria create friction without improving lead quality

examples.text: Alex Hormozi replaced a non-converting webinar with a free case study video titled 'How We Added 213 Members to a Gym and $112,000 in San Diego.' The morning after he made the swap, his partner Layla's calendar was full. He attributed the result to the case study being a lower-friction, self-paced format that more sophisticated business-owner audiences would consume without perceiving it as a sales pitch — unlike a webinar, which more advanced audiences recognize as a sales vehicle and therefore resist.

Alex Hormozi ran a campaign for Gym Launch's software company (Allen) with the lead magnet titled 'Four Reasons Why You'll Never Have a Million Dollar Agency.' The ad targeted small SMB lead generation agencies and revealed four specific blockers to the $1M milestone. Prospects who recognized themselves in all four reasons assumed Hormozi could help solve them, generating high-quality opt-ins among the exact target avatar. The reveal-a-problem frame increased deprivation for the outcome (million-dollar agency) that the audience most wanted.

When Alex Hormozi ran Gym Launch, new gym owners would purchase a monetization system (how to make the gym more profitable) and simultaneously receive four months of free agency lead generation services. After four months of having leads delivered automatically, owners were accustomed to the flow. When Hormozi then charged for continued lead services, the deprivation created by the upcoming removal of free leads converted them into paying customers without resistance.

For his first personal training business, Alex Hormozi trained clients for free for one year, calling it the Free Training Project, with the goal of accumulating testimonials. After a year of delivering results, demand exceeded capacity. He asked all free clients if they wanted to continue as paying customers; almost all said yes. He used this to counter the objection that free offers attract only freebie seekers — the right qualified free recipients convert to paid customers when results are delivered.

Alex Hormozi described a B2B website-speed-audit lead magnet: offer a free site speed test to business owners. Upon testing, if the site loads in nine seconds, the auditor explains that every additional second of load time costs approximately 3% in conversion rate — meaning cutting load time from nine to three seconds would yield an 18% conversion increase. Relative to the business's revenue, the cost of the website fix is negligible, creating a strong purchase case at the moment of maximum deprivation (the prospect now knows exactly how much they are losing per second of delay).

Alex Hormozi described a physical product lead magnet at a conference: give away a t-shirt or hat printed with 'CEO' only to people who prove they are a CEO. The physical product qualifies the audience naturally (only actual CEOs want the CEO shirt) and leaves Hormozi with a list of verified, ego-identified executives for approximately $3-4 per t-shirt. Assuming one in twenty converts to a customer, the effective CAC is $60-80 for a CEO-level lead, which Hormozi characterized as a good deal.

Alex Hormozi described a fashion personal stylist named Ashley whose website displayed only a book-a-call CTA. After analyzing her traffic (cold, low-awareness), Hormozi recommended replacing or supplementing the direct CTA with a lead magnet — something that delivers early value (e.g., a personalized color palette) and then reveals the follow-on problem (how do I combine colors into outfits?) that Ashley's full styling service solves. This is an example of the one-step-of-many lead magnet type applied to a service business.

Alex Hormozi described the naming of his gym's free workout program: instead of calling it a 'Six-Week Deadlift and Squat Seminar' (accurate but unappealing to his primary audience of women), he named it 'Big Booty Bootcamp.' The actual content was identical — primarily deadlifts, squats, and hip thrusts. The rename dramatically increased opt-ins from his target avatar. He used this to illustrate that the vehicle (exercise protocol) should not be advertised — the result (desired physical outcome) should be.

Alex Hormozi described his $100M Leads book naming process: he split tested six different headline options before publication, and additionally tested the cover image and sub-headlines. He described spending two days testing headlines for a book that took two years to write, arguing that the headline would influence more short-term purchases than any content improvement — while long-term sales would ultimately be driven by word of mouth based on the content quality.

practices.text: Insert a lead magnet between cold traffic and your core offer CTA; the lead magnet should solve a narrow problem related to but not identical to the problem your core offer solves.

Test lead magnet headlines by polling your existing audience (stories, texts, posts) or running small paid split tests; use at least two or three data sources to get a directional answer before committing.
Add a qualification dropdown or conditional form redirect to your lead magnet opt-in so that only qualified prospects (budget, authority, need, timing) receive the high-value free offer.
Embed CTAs within the lead magnet itself and immediately before and after delivery — not just at the end — to maximize the number of times you ask without changing the ask-to-value ratio.

State genuine capacity limits in service business CTAs (e.g., four open spots this month) rather than leaving them unstated; prospects do not know your business size and will not assume scarcity exists unless you say so.

For the Reveal-a-Problem lead magnet type, quantify the delta between the prospect's current state and the improved state after your core offer is applied, and show that the cost of your offer is small relative to the value of the gap.

When delivering free services as a lead magnet, limit delivery to prospects who confirm budget, authority, need, and timing before the free work begins — treat qualification as a prerequisite to access, not a post-delivery filter.
